findings.title: Bash script uses `set +e` instead of `set -euo pipefail`
findings.description: The file opens with `set +e`, which explicitly disables exit-on-error. The template standard is unambiguous: 'All scripts must start with `set -euo pipefail`.' The logging-never-breaks-a-tool-call invariant is a valid reason to deviate, but the template requires an inline ignore with a justification comment when a rule 'truly can't be fixed.' The current file has a prose comment ('Logging failures NEVER break a tool call') but it is not structured as a justified deviation from `set -euo pipefail` — it merely explains intent, not why the rule is being overridden. The correct form is `set -uo pipefail` (like peer files `log-rotate.sh`, `safety-block.sh`) with a justification comment, or the current `set +e` with an explicit override comment.
findings.rule_citation: claude-md-template.md, Bash section: 'All scripts must start with `set -euo pipefail`.' and Comments policy: 'If a warning truly can't be fixed, add an inline ignore with a justification comment.'

findings.title: Multiple new Bash scripts use `set -uo pipefail` instead of `set -euo pipefail`
findings.description: Nine new or modified Bash scripts open with `set -uo pipefail`, omitting the `-e` flag. The standard requires `set -euo pipefail` for all scripts. Some of these files (safety-block.sh, safety-warn.sh) need graceful exit-0 fallbacks for error paths, but those are handled with explicit `|| echo ""` or `2>/dev/null || echo` patterns — they do not require disabling `-e` globally. The test scripts have no stated reason to omit `-e`. None of the files include an inline comment justifying the deviation.

findings.title: Sourced Bash library has no `set` directive and no justification comment
findings.description: `hooks/lib/common.sh` is a sourced helper with no `set` directive at all. While sourced libraries conventionally omit `set -euo pipefail` (to avoid affecting the sourcing script's state), the template rule is unqualified. The template's zero-warnings policy says deviations require an inline comment with justification. There is no such comment explaining why the `set` directive is absent.

findings.title: Nine commit subject lines exceed the 72-character limit
findings.description:
The template requires '<=72 char subject line' for commits. Nine commits in this PR exceed that limit:
- `feat(validate): verify symlinks, log dir, hook executability, settings hooks block` (82 chars)
- `docs(readme): add Logging + Anti-rationalization sections; updated file structure` (81 chars)
- `perf(log-tool-calls): consolidate into single python3 process; pair by input hash` (81 chars)
- `feat(install): hybrid mode — symlinks for content, jq-merge for settings.json` (79 chars)
- `docs(claude-md): add Go section, output preferences, comments policy, pointers` (78 chars)
- `docs: add PROMOTION-RATIONALE.md explaining why no resurgent items went global` (78 chars)
- `docs(readme): bump retention reference 90 → 365 days to match log-rotate.sh` (77 chars)
- `test: add test-redaction.sh covering all secret patterns + adversarial input` (76 chars)
- `feat(settings): wire log/safety/anti-rat/log-rotate hooks; extend allow list` (76 chars)

findings.title: Comment explains WHAT the fallback does, not WHY
findings.description: Lines 195-196 read: `# Post: pair by content hash. Fall back to most-recent same-session` / `# file (handles the case where pre-row was missing).` The first clause ('pair by content hash') restates what the code is already doing. The second clause ('handles the case where pre-row was missing') describes a code path rather than explaining a non-obvious constraint. The comments policy says 'Don't explain WHAT the code does — well-named identifiers already do that.' The WHY (pre-rows can be absent if the hook was added mid-session) is legitimate but not stated. Moderate confidence because the boundary between WHAT and WHY is partly a judgment call here.
findings.rule_citation: claude-md-template.md, Comments policy: 'Don't explain WHAT the code does — well-named identifiers already do that.'

findings.title: Section-divider comments use WHAT-labeling style
findings.description: The file uses visual section dividers like `# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------` / `# Redaction patterns (kept in sync with hooks/lib/redact.py)` and `# JSONL write with truncation (kept in sync with hooks/lib/jsonl-write.py)` and `# Hook entry`. These reference callers ('kept in sync with hooks/lib/redact.py') and label sections by WHAT they are. The comments policy explicitly prohibits 'Don't reference the current task, fix, or callers ("used by X", "added for the Y flow").' The 'kept in sync' annotation is a caller reference that will rot as the codebase evolves. Moderate-low confidence because section dividers in a long single-file module arguably serve structural navigation, but the caller-reference content is a clear violation.

findings.title: `_redact_value` lacks return type annotation; `_truncate_output` parameter types are incomplete
findings.description: The template Python stack uses `ty check` for static types and requires 'Google-style docstrings on non-trivial public APIs'. The function `_redact_value(v)` has no type annotations on its parameter or return value. `_truncate_output(obj: dict, max_bytes: int) -> dict` uses bare `dict` rather than `dict[str, Any]`. These are private functions (underscore prefix) so 'public API' does not strictly apply, but `ty` will flag the untyped `v` parameter in strict mode. Confidence is moderate-low because the template's type annotation requirement is stated for 'public APIs' and these are private helpers.

residual_risks.description: The `|| true` wrapping on all logging paths in `log-tool-calls.sh` (via `exec python3 ...` with `set +e`) means Python import errors or missing `lib/log_tool_call.py` at the symlinked path will silently produce no log output and no user-visible error. If `SCRIPT_DIR` resolution fails (edge: broken symlink with no fallback), the `exec` will exit non-zero but `set +e` suppresses that. A startup-time sanity check (e.g., checking the python file exists before exec) would surface misconfigured installs without breaking tool calls.

The `install_settings` jq merge uses `$existing * $new` (object merge) which for nested objects performs a shallow merge. If the existing `settings.json` has a `PreToolUse` hooks block and the new one also has a `PreToolUse` block, the merge replaces the array entirely rather than appending. The code then does `.hooks = ($existing.hooks // {}) * ($new.hooks // {})` which shallow-merges — a user who had custom hooks in the existing `PreToolUse` block would lose them. This is not a style violation but a correctness risk.

testing_gaps.description: `tests/test-hooks.sh` checks `safety-block.sh` against two cases (safe command, rm -rf /Users/somebody). The full 16-block + 9-allow matrix from `test-safety-block.sh` (Task 7 smoke test in the plan) is NOT replicated in the final `tests/test-hooks.sh`. The plan's smoke test was run during development but its assertions are not part of the permanent test suite, so regressions in fork-bomb, dd, mkfs, fdisk, wipefs, chmod-777, and force-push patterns are untested in CI.

`log_tool_call.py` is the consolidated single-process replacement for the bash+pipeline approach but has no dedicated unit tests in `tests/`. The `tests/test-hooks.sh` exercises it end-to-end via `bash hooks/log-tool-calls.sh pre`, but the truncation logic, MCP parsing, pair-key hashing, and duration calculation are only covered by the high-level integration path. A unit test similar to the `test_jsonl_smoke.py` inline test in the plan would give confidence that the consolidated code behaves identically to the two separate files it replaced.
